title: Argentina edge Brazil in a World Cup 2026 classic
summary: Lionel Messi's brilliance and two clinical second-half goals saw Argentina defeat Brazil 2-1 in an all-time World Cup 2026 group-stage classic.
content:
A packed MetLife Stadium fell silent for a fraction of a second before erupting as Julián Álvarez's 71st-minute header sealed a famous 2-1 victory for Argentina over Brazil in what may already be the defining match of the 2026 FIFA World Cup group stage. From the first whistle to the last, the encounter delivered everything a global audience could have wished for: attacking intent, tactical intrigue and the inescapable magnetism of football's oldest continental rivalry.

Messi sets the tone

Lionel Messi, wearing the captain's armband for what could be his final World Cup, gave Argentina the lead in the 23rd minute with a finish of almost contemptuous simplicity. Receiving the ball with his back to goal just inside the penalty area, he turned Marquinhos with a deft shoulder drop and curled a right-footed shot into the far corner past a helpless Ederson. The MetLife crowd — a sea of sky-blue and white — rose as one. Brazil responded with characteristic resilience, and Vinícius Júnior levelled matters just before the break with a darting run in behind the defence and a cool finish across Emiliano Martínez.

Second-half intensity

The interval brought no respite to the frantic pace. Brazil's head coach pushed Rodrygo higher after the restart, and for twenty minutes they pinned Argentina back, forcing Martínez into a sharp one-handed stop from a Raphinha free-kick. Argentina's reprieve came from their most reliable source: Messi driving forward from deep, drawing two defenders before threading a precise pass into the channel for Álvarez, who met it with a thumping header at the near post. It was Álvarez's fourth goal of the tournament and a reminder of why Pep Guardiola fought so hard to keep him at Manchester City.

Brazil push for an equaliser

Losing this fixture was not in Brazil's script, and they threw men forward in the final quarter-hour with Endrick, the youngest player in either squad, entering the fray. His pace troubled Argentina's defensive line repeatedly, and only a last-ditch block from Cristian Romero denied him a debut World Cup goal. Argentina, though, managed the clock expertly, circulating possession with the composure of champions, running down the seconds until Facundo Medina's final whistle clearance brought the full-time signal.

Statistics tell the story

Argentina edged the expected-goals battle 1.82 to 1.54, reflecting the efficiency with which they converted their chances. Brazil dominated possession at 58% and registered 14 shots to Argentina's 9, yet they were undone by two moments of individual brilliance at either end — Messi's opener and Álvarez's winner. The match illustrated a perennial truth about top-level football: raw numbers matter less than composure at the decisive moment.

With this result Argentina lead Group C with six points from two games, while Brazil must beat Iran in their final group fixture to advance. For the spectators fortunate enough to have a ticket — and for the hundreds of millions watching worldwide — this was an evening that justified every superlative the sport has to offer. Sunday night at MetLife was, quite simply, why the World Cup exists.
